title: Teaching Machines to Listen Like People, Only Better
summary:
The crack of a bat and the roar of a crowd can tell a baseball fan something exciting just happened, even without seeing the home run. Humans may be visual creatures, but we also learn about the world by listening. At MIT, Professor Paris Smaragdis wants to build machines that can hear and understand sound even better than humans.

A machine with super-human hearing could pinpoint a traffic accident by listening for squealing tires and crunching metal, or identify when an industrial drill might break while boring through dense bedrock to dig a geothermal well. As Smaragdis puts it, he does the same thing computer vision researchers do, but for hearing.

Smaragdis, who joined MIT in 2025, leads a research group exploring machine learning for sound source separation, smart devices that can augment people's audio surroundings, and better tools to help people understand, manipulate, analyze, and create music.

His path began with music. He grew up in Greece and began playing classical guitar. A turning point came when his father brought home a synthesizer that let him make sounds. At Berklee College of Music in Boston, he explored computers and synthesizers to shape sound, and majored in bass.

With mentor Richard Boulanger, he created tools to help people use computers to write, produce, and enhance music, then worked with Professor Barry Vercoe at the MIT Media Lab on software synthesizers.

In the Media Lab, his attention shifted to making computers understand sound. Many students then used signal processing to help machines handle sound, but Smaragdis chose the less explored approach of machine learning. We need to teach computers how to listen, he concluded, because we cannot simply tell them how: we lack a vocabulary to explain listening, or how to tell a cat's meow from a violin.
why_it_matters: Machines that truly understand sound could warn people about danger sooner and help people hear their surroundings more clearly, from busy streets to workplaces.

background_read: Machine listening is the work of teaching computers to make sense of sounds, in the same way computer vision teaches them to make sense of images.

A computer cannot simply be told how to listen, because people do not have a ready set of words to explain how they tell one sound from another, so researchers teach machines by showing them many examples.
Smaragdis came to this work through music, first playing and shaping sounds with instruments and computers, and later turning to how machines themselves can understand sound.
His group now explores tools that separate sounds, improve the sounds around people, and help people work with music.
